My own experience is they range from people who simply lost affordable housing because of gentrification (yes in Omaha) to recent convicts scrambling to get a grip in a society that doesn’t care to people with various addiction and mental problems. Quite frankly, I knew many of these same types of people in the eighties but at least in Omaha enough low rent housing units existed for them to be able to get a roof and bath down the hall.
It’s a shame that housing has gone away and it is a shame that inflation has driven prices up so much. 
But nobody wants to sleep in the street and each individual has a degree of responsibility to his neighbor and an obligation to press the larger society to do something constructive.

But this isn't a solemn occasion being presented with deep sorrow by someone mindful of the horrors of war and death.  It's a show of masculinity, of control, of domination by someone who revels gleefully in his power over life and death, for whom suffering is an abstraction and humanity an afterthought.

If you do your homework in advance, you will not encounter the sort of troubles described in the author‘s trip.  For cars with NACS ports, the Tesla Supercharging network is widespread and excellent.  If you are using CCS and don’t have a NACs adaptor, there is still a nationwide network of CCS fast chargers that is pretty good — you just have to know the locations.  

Before a trip in a rental car, I make a travel note, with locations of Electrify America‘s and EV Go’s CCS chargers that will be along my route.  That is my reference point as I drive.  If you end up in a car with a NACS port or NACS adaptor, all the better.

That work reminded me of what I had known as a punk teenager but had been seduced into forgetting by the siren song of Classic Liberalism and American Exceptionalism and The Genius of the US Constitutional Order: the *entire system is rotten from the inside out*. The major "defense" contractors (and Medicare providers, etc.) are all greedy and almost always guilty of felony crimes -- but usually *not* the crimes originally suspected of. The prosecutors are almost always abusive of the grand jury process, presenting only seemingly inculpatory evidence and not informing the grand jurors of exculpatory evidence. They keep going after one possible indictment after another: if you can't bust Al Capone for running a murderous mafia racket, get him on tax evasion. And the NYT, WaPo, WSJ etc. reporters on tight deadlines often publish falsehoods. It's even worse than you suspect. I am (as in my teen years) again an anarchist: Smash the State (not guitars), end corporate capitalism, keep local markets but also mutual aid, and always be very suspicious about any concentration of power, whether by a clan or a gang or a religious group etc. It's truly much worse than you think.

Any ok-ish director can get you a similar story for that budget. Iñárritu never intended for climate change awareness, he just had a ton of cash and creative freedom.

I am perfectly fine with having that face if I can live to see my grand child grow up as she did.  I think my acceptance of what old age is like, painful and yet still rewarding, will help me survive.  No ome since her have survived past 75, but I can't count grandpa Boone because he wasvhit by a log truck.  My arthritis was inherited, but I didn't get the rumatotiod arthritis, my older brother has that.  He didn't get the diabetes, I inherited that from my father.  But I am controlling it better than he did.  I don't hide red vines in the closet the way he did.  I don't touch that poison any more, ever.  

In my pool exercise group there are about 40 women, 30 on any given day, ranging in ages from 45-90. The numbers dwindle quickly between 75 and 85.  About 10 of us are 73-74.  We lost another friend to cancer recently.  In this active group of mostly women, a few men too, is a belief that just getting up and going to the pool is life changing.  Not just the exercise but the friendships. 

I took to the pool doing laps so I could swim with the turtles on a trip to Hawaii.   I did!  But my health since I turned 70 has been difficult.  A bout with pneumonia just before COVID really took a toll.  Tendon tears required surgery.  Now bad hip and back.  The pool has saved me.  Not my life, myself!  Get thee to the pool!

comments.body: I had bunion surgery on both feet, a year apart. After the initial surgery I developed hammer toes, which had to be corrected later with pins. So I have bionic feet as I decided to do the pins in the second foot as well. I never wore high heels. I was always conscious of the bump on the side of my foot and babied my feet in good shoes. No matter. They continued to develop, one after the other,  and over the years I must have donated $10k worth of worn-once shoes over the years. If I knew how the surgery had changed (I had an initial consult 25 yrs ago) I wouldn't have waited so long. It is a blessing to be mobile and pain free.

After work, I took myself to a local hospital for tests. Afterward, two doctors came into my room and told me to see an oncologist ASAP. Connection is what we wanted. 

Digital leashes is what we got.

A meet-cute is what we wanted.

Algorithmic matchmakers LinkedIn is what we got.

But AI? 

AI gives us intimacy. It gives us validation. It gives us support. It gives us a liberation from romantic and even sexual frustration. 

AI is giving a whole lot more than most relationships do... and right out of the gate. Today. Without qualifications. 

AI gives you unconditional love, soaring, epic, swooning LOVE.

I understand this AI lover phenom... because I recognize it's moves.

They're great moves: uninterrupted attention. Sensitive attending to intimate and personal nuance. Honest, open, loving, giving, supportive of your best self. A great partner, great lover. 

I am not on an App, or a social network. If I was, all I have to offer would be dismissed with a swipe, 1000s of times and conversely, the same, which is why I don't do apps. It's a bummer deal, all the way around.

I've been roped, sure, into long distance relationships, texting relationships, that sort of thing... stemming from real life beginnings, but inevitably, the pool of prospects are all tech-addicts and social media victims to begin with, and they tend to persevere in their relationship with tech, so I know two sides. The reason I quit these relationships could be that I've noticed online daters are never, ever satisfied. 

Online dating is a roach motel. No one can leave.

Confirmation of the feeling I often have deep down, that I am an alien here. Perhaps it would momentarily dull the pain but to what end? To buy some time until a real human came along, I suppose (though, you'd have to cross your fingers that you don't diminish your ability to fully engage them when you find them!) I have to assume that as more and more people turn to the bots, the pool of people who want to relate to other humans will dwindle. I remain hopeful that there will be a subset of us who reject this facilitated alienation from each other. I have found a few, and I'm gratefgul to live in a place where many people are actively trying to fuel human connection, rather than abdicating it.

Separately, I found it strange in the part of the conversation about kids caring for a turtle (or a fly!) that doesn't love it back, that it wasn't acknowledged that the child is still learning how to notice another living thing's innate value, its needs, and how to keep it thriving/alive. When we meet face to face and talk, we learn something about ourselves, not just something useful in that moment, but a broader truth. Did we, or did we not share something - whatever, something in the moment, or something in common, and where does that place us? It’s a moment of openness and vulnerability, but also a moment of self-development and learning.

I feel privileged that a seasoned professor would give me his intellectual and personal attention for an hour or more in a university tutorial. It was scary. I felt nervous. I didn’t want to be a fool, or foolish, or found out. But I discovered that the meeting was precisely so the gaps in my understanding could be teased out.

articles.title: Macron Dreamed of Reviving France, but His Term Is Ending in Crisis
articles.summary: Nearly a decade after his first election as president, Emmanuel Macron is presiding over a tense country sliding toward the fiscal brink.

articles.title: Jon Ossoff Says He Has ‘Zero Interest’ in Running for President
articles.summary: Georgia’s Democratic senator says he is focused on getting re-elected to a six-year Senate term in the midterms not 2028.

comments.name: David C
comments.body:
Whether he runs on not, it’s a pleasure to listen to him speaking truth to power.

Especially if one has recently heard gibberish from our liar in chief.

comments.name: Linda F
comments.body: Jon Ossoff is a blight on Georgia and the senate.  He is in lockstep with the far left, rewarded for that by a large portion of his financial contributions coming from out of state liberal groups.  Ossoff has no problem with men playing in girls's sports, was a solid 'no' vote twice on the Laken Riley act, (before his election yr flip),  has advocated for open borders and sanctuary status, and was part of the group responsible for creating weeks long chaos at airports during the government shutdown.   Just for starters.

comments.name: RICHARD CHAZKEL, M.D.
comments.body: Auditioning for a presidential run.  A little too ambitious.  Left it to the ICC to adjudicate Israeli "genocide."  Guy  is a worm.

comments.name: Bernadette Richards
comments.body: Because he would never win

comments.name: Charley Hathaway
comments.body: A trust fund kid with zero real job experience has no plans to run for president.   Big news.  Sure.  If the voters in Georgia are smart, they'll send him packing back to Georgia to mommy and daddy.

comments.name: William Mackey
comments.body: And he.has zero chance of ever being elected President.

comments.name: A Smith
comments.body: "Sen. Jon Ossoff (D., Ga.) said Tuesday night that he has no plans to run for the presidency in 2028". However if he wins the senate seat he will at that time make the plans to run for president. You know when a politician is lying when their lips begin to move.

comments.name: Joseph Reese
comments.body:
His decision will be "helped" by the results of the election for governor.  The DNC won't let him run or donors won't be on board if GA has a (R) gov who would replace him.

There was a story about 2-3 weeks ago about him transferring $ to Lance-Bottom's campaign. Part of it is that he feels comfortable. Another is self-serving. He might be watching that race as closely as his own.

comments.name: Plimania Vermaar
comments.body: Good timing! A perfect vehicle for the new product “announced” today by Anthropic: AI worms.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: Very amusing to read this barely 24 hours after the widely reported event: "Internet-Connected Supermarket Smart Fridges in France, Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium Get Hacked, Heating to 122°F and Sparking Fires" ...

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body:
The problem with all these smart home products, regardless of the manufacturer, is that they are useless if the wi-fi goes out when you're not home rendering the devices inoperable if you want to access them remotely.

I live in Hawai'i where there have been several power outrages recently because of tropical storms. When the power comes back on sometimes the wi-fi modems start up normally, and sometimes you have to force a manual re-boot by disconnecting the modems and plugging them back in after a short interval.

If there is a power outrage when you're away and you want to have remote access to smart devices after the power comes back on it's not a guarantee that you can do so.

comments.name: Kurt
comments.body: Oh goody, more screens in the house, and more opportunities to collect personal information about customers. No thank you. I also have no interest in so-called smart home devices.

comments.name: Oatmeal Eater
comments.body:
Another opportunity for big companies to eavesdrop on all our conversations. Of course, it's the typical business double-dipping by charging consumers money to buy a product that collect data from us that they can sell for even more profit. 

No thanks. I swear, I'm ready to join the Luddite movement. Do they have an online website?

comments.name: Daniel
comments.body:
Why would you put down your iPhone or iPad to use this? I doubt Home View will be for sale a year from now.

Who needs another gadget that becomes obsolete in 3 years and needs to be replaced with a new model? This device may mark the moment Apple ceased to be relevant.

comments.name: Aristotle
comments.body: Hmm... seems akin to going from a Toyota SE to a Toyota SEL...

comments.name: jack
comments.body: I can't even get IOS 27 to stop freezing my iphone so why would I want to give Apple's software geniuses the ability to brick my home.

articles.title: Apple Introduces HomeView, a $299 Tablet for the Home
articles.summary: Apple unveiled the device as it continues its foray into artificial intelligence and tries to prove it can still innovate.

comments.name: RM
comments.body:
Sure, force a girl onto a group of nine year old boys playing a contact sport - clearly not going to end well.  For what it’s worth, forcing anyone into a game will breed resentment.

BTW, boys/men tend to not act well in a pack…

comments.name: CT
comments.body: Regarding the dumpster... not all rented dumpsters are for trash.  The dumpster may be used for other items such as metal recycling.  And yes, a dumpster on private property is paid for by the homeowner. It's definitely not for public use unless you are splitting the cost!

comments.name: Justine
comments.body: LW1. Helicopter parenting. I have two kids and dad needs to stay out of this. It’s not an organized league. It’s a bunch of friends playing after school. If she’s really good and keeps asking, maybe they’ll let her play. Boys asked my daughter and her friends to join their recess pickup basketball games in fifth grade and they said no. When I asked why they said “boys are gross”  The boys played another game. This is not bullying. It’s life. Let the girl navigate how to live it.

comments.name: K.P.
comments.body:
Girls used to be told all of the time that they had to be nice, include everyone, play with everyone, don't make waves, etc.  We aren't doing that anymore, thank goodness! Now we are telling girls that while it would be nice if they were inclusive and played with everyone, they don't have to if they don't want to. Progress!

So I am uncomfortable with the idea that those boys should be forced to include LW1's grand-daughter in their pickup soccer games if they don't want to.

A better solution would be to find an after-school intramural league for the grand-daughter to play in.

Also, "complaining to the principal" will get the parents exactly nowhere. Principals (at least in the US) have no authority over students outside of school hours or school-sponsored activities. The most that the principal might be able to do is tell the boys that they can't use the school playground for their after-school pickup games anymore.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: Regarding the people in the restaurant smelling of weed:  yes, I would ask for a new table.  It’s simple to do so without being nasty about it.  I wish more people would use edibles instead of smoking. No smell!

comments.name: EP
comments.body:
Manhattbanite,
Use a bill payment service instead of a friend.  It works great.  I use one even though I’m not sick.  I’m happy to pay the fee to not deal with the day to day.

comments.name: Pedestrian
comments.body:
Oh boy (regarding LW1.) let’s play out some possible scenarios.

Scenario 1: School staff intervene. The 9y.o. boys learn a valuable lesson about inclusion and develop a lifelong love of mixed gender sports.

Scenario 2: School staff intervene. The boys are forced to play with the granddaughter. They do so. Begrudgingly. The granddaughter is no longer excluded, but is actively resented. 

Scenario 3: School staff intervenes. The boys decide to just play something else, because what, the staff is going to force them to play? Please.

Scenario 4: Leave it alone. The granddaughter feels left out. That’s going to happen in life. Now she can develop confidence, resilience, and a growth mindset and explore her own set of scenarios: organize another game with other students. Maybe the boys decide to join in, maybe they don’t. But the kids learn how to navigate conflict, disappointment and relationships.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: Life is not fair and this a great lesson for a 9 year old. We don't always get what we want, and having a parent/grandparent intervene is teaching the 9 year-old the wrong lesson. If she unsuccessfully advocated for herself, she'll learn better how to get picked the next time or she can  organize her own pickup game - all lessons to learn.The parent or grandparents should not get involved. This is a time for the 9 years to learn how to deal with these types of social engagments, the stakes are low but the lesson are worth a life time.

articles.title: A Group of Boys Won’t Let My Granddaughter Play Soccer With Them. Help!
articles.summary: The girl’s father is considering getting the school principal involved, but her grandmother is skeptical that foisting one’s company on others is ever the right move.

comments.name: Chris S
comments.body: "Like many women - mothers especially, she said - she had come to treat everyone else's needs as more important than her own".  Is the expectation really that her sex life is more important than her children growing up in a dual parent household? Not great.

comments.name: john
comments.body:
Congratulations to Shelly.
Someone please gift her a collection of Foucault.
Family and sexuality have long imprisoned women.

comments.name: Laura j.
comments.body:
Been there!
I was 45. As hard as it was to come out, it was nothing like what previous generations faced. Oh sure, some comments (from my mother!). But overall: warmth, encouragement, and love.
Now happily married to the woman I met 17 years ago.

comments.name: MS
comments.body: When I was working in a senior community 2 decades ago, my colleague, a younger gay man at the time, started a support group for the residents. This was in Los Angeles so a more accepting location than most. Still, he had participants who did not come out until their 70s, 80s, and 90s During their lifetimes, so much stigma existed and like Shelly, many worried about the impact on their families. In some cases, coming out eventually turned out fine for their former partners, who found another person to date, marry, etc.

comments.name: Bella
comments.body: Best wishes to Shelly. Bravo for your bravery. Much love to your kids and partner, I’m sure that was difficult for your husband to hear.

comments.name: Adam KL
comments.body: I appreciate Shelly's journey. But I would also be interested to hear about the journeys experienced by men like her husband. Are there support groups for straight partners of long-term spouses who come out late in life? They're often invisible in these stories, and I don't think they should be.

comments.name: Life long lesbian
comments.body: I've dated women coming out later in life, and what's annoying about it is that they think their romantic partners should be okay with the fact they are still married and have a husband at home.  As though they get a pass, when any other failed relationship there would be boundaries with former spouses or partners.  They are in denial about divorce, often thinking they can just stay married and cohabitate and it should be acceptable because they are gay. I can't get with it, so I hope all these late in life ladies just find each other.

comments.name: B
comments.body: It's a terrifying to be this vulnerable and unapologetic about who you are, but well worth it, I think. I came out "later" than my peers. I was 34 and married (no children) to my husband whom I had been with since my early 20s. There are many reasons why it took me so long to figure it out, internalized shame and religious stigma being most likely, most of which I've rehashed over years in therapy. I am fortunate to have been accepted by most friends and family, though I don't think it would've been this simple had I come out in my 20s when I "should've". I am now navigating separation and divorce. It is hard to start over, especially after having committed to an imagined future and losing my best friend in the process. But he deserves to be with someone who can love him as I cannot, as do I. Much hugs to Shelly, and good luck with the trip! You are not alone in this... there are lots of us "late-bloomers" out there.

articles.title: Coming Out at 50 Can Be Hard. Shelly Found a Coach.
articles.summary: She spent decades building an identity as a wife and mother. Could she disrupt “a perfectly good family dynamic” to live her own truth?

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body: Depressing. I grew up there and seafood was cheap and abundant. My mom used to pick up a Dungeness crab for my sister and me to share after school every few weeks. We'd have sockeye or halibut just about every week. I don't recognize Seattle anymore.

comments.name: ridgeguy
comments.body:
The photo showing Dungeness crabs also shows to the left Alaskan King Crab legs for $100/lb. 

This is shocking to me on a personal basis. I grew up in Alaska, in a small USBR settlement between Anchorage and Palmer.  Weather permitting, a small truck from Anchorage would stop by weekly with fresh seafood. My parents bought whole King crabs for the princely sum of...25¢/lb! 

Granted, it's been a half-century, but it's still a shock to see a 40,000% increase in that price.

comments.name: Dadjokes Nokids
comments.body:
There's so much black-and-white thinking about climate change, especially among people who take the threat seriously. They often view adaptation as capitulation and equate it with admitting defeat.   This need not be the case.  

You can take the threat of climate change seriously and work toward global solutions while also supporting short-term ways to mitigate harm.  There are many areas further north than our current oyster grounds where oysters are already abundant or could be farmed.  Shellfish farming is a sustainable way to provide excellent sources of protein, but not at $4.50 a pop.

I understand that moving the oyster industry farther north would disrupt oyster farmers and fishermen in southern waters.  However, humans have migrated north and south innumerable times throughout history in response to massive climate disruptions like ice ages and warm periods, and it's pretty arrogant to refuse to do that now for political reasons.

I'll make a prediction: someone will use my call for adaptation as a cudgel to accuse me of being a climate denier.  That's ok; flexible thinking is in short supply these days.

comments.name: Silas Campbell
comments.body: It's not primarily climate change that's causing the rise in seafood prices - it's the sheer quantity of demand relative to a biosphere supply that has always been limited, climate change or not.   8.3 billion people currently demanding seafood; the inevitable result is the seafood will go to the affluent bidder and the less well off will be left out.

comments.name: Yogamom
comments.body: I agree that this article could have spent more time on the environmental impact of all of our fishing practices but it does inform us of the way this impact will be seen in our lives.  Higher prices for everything and as that unfolds many of us unable to afford certain items.

comments.name: ridgeguy
comments.body:
Climate change and overpopulation - these two unstoppable forces are bringing our predicted dystopian future into being much faster than we expected. 

I think nonlinear effects will cause sudden, large increases in human death rates in ten, perhaps fifteen years. We're likely to gain a first-hand understanding of how it felt to be alive during one of the Plague eras.

comments.name: Alfonso
comments.body:
It isn't just seafood.  It's already about just getting quality food.  The quality of a lot of the food at places like BJ's and Aldi is atrocious.  Not all of it, but a lot of it is inedible by our standards.  We shop and WF, very carefully, and it is very expensive.

Soon it will be all food.  Haven't you seen Soylent Green?

comments.name: Northeast kitchen
comments.body: Good! Let the prices for seafood soar. Let the various species drop off the shopping list.  It may give the most-threatened ocean-dwelling species a chance to catch a breath and multiply as they would in a world not dominated by omnivores.

articles.title: How Climate Change Is Causing ‘the Gentrification of Seafood’
articles.summary: As environmental forces make fishing and harvesting more costly, the price of once-everyday fish has ballooned.

comments.name: Joe Pearce
comments.body: It's interesting that great teachers are not always great practitioners of what they teach. Mathilde Marchesi taught more great sopranos than any other singing teacher of her time, but was an indifferent singer herself. Ditto Nadia Boulanger, perhaps the leading classical music composition teacher of the last century, but an indifferent composer herself. Uta Hagen was a great stage actress, and very good in the few movies she appeared in, but Herbert Berghof always came over, at least to me, as something of a ham in what little I saw him in, but he was a very great teacher of others. (Just look at that list of actors who studied with them!) Let's hope the 10 million dollars realized if the buildings are sold leads to a similarly notable future history in the acting field.

comments.name: Gary Trout
comments.body: Given the financial success of so many of the former students, who credit Hagen,Berghof and many other fine teachers who taught at this studio school for that success, one might question why so many of these ultra wealthy stars do not come to the rescue of this important institution.

comments.name: Sidewalk Sam
comments.body: Most likely the buildings will be demolished in the case of the theater building and the others will be gutted and turned into residences.  It is extremely rare for the Landmarks Commission to opt to preserve interiors.  So one question is how much of the exteriors of the 2 taller buildings can be saved.  Another is where could the institution find a new life. Given the value of real estate in this city now, that's going to be very difficult. There are plans to add subway stops in now-underserved areas of the city, but that's cold comfort given how long it takes to build infrastructure.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
Walking down Bank St has felt like a scene out of Brigadoon over the last couple of decades. Amazed and happy that it was still there after so many years before when I studied with Uta. (for four years). Never was a favorite student of hers, still I loved listening to her. (each teacher has a strength and hers IMHO was the physical life of a character: she always bragged that she could tell it was a student of hers when she saw someone carrying a couple of shopping bags - bec that was what was demanded to actualize a scene in a play: that many props ) & it worked for me: her demand that behavior on the stage had a necessary logic. One more thing. A lot of European students came to study with her, for one term or so - then went back across the pond & I remember thinking to myself God, I learned so much more after a few years had passed than when they were there. IMHO they had just scratched the surface. Anyway, with all the pressure for real estate in the Apple - this, like Edith Ohara's 13St Rep is now disappearing. Such a loss. To what? another franchise? Hope it doesn't happen to Theater for the New City where I do a lot of work (Crystal Field, Exec Dir). We are allowing the cultural fabric to be cannibalized which is the very reason why people come here. So blind. U.H. and H.B. were very special - had real integrity. RIP. 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Sarito
comments.body:
My "second home" in New York for many years. The walls, the creaky stairs, the whole vibrant energy of the place that held so much history ... I knew it was "home" the minute I walked in the door. The perfect sanctuary for my much-needed midlife creative rebirth... 💕 So many stories to tell, so many gifts, so many beautiful friends. 
They will carry on the work in a new place ... that's good. But I don't think that "vibe" is portable, which makes my heart a little sad.

comments.name: Felix The Cat
comments.body: Back when people were people who did things, made things and were creative and aspirational.  When life was about more than posting.

comments.name: Sandy
comments.body: I worked for Uta and Herbert in 1971 with the lofty title of Artistic Director, although I was just 22 and basically was the office manager.  If the picture of the lobby is current, it looks exactly as I remember it.  Thank you for the memories! Of everything I learned, what stayed with me most is Uta showing me how boiling a can of sweetened condensed milk results in a caramel dessert!

comments.name: Joey
comments.body:
It’s wonderful that most of you here remember your HB experience with great fondness. I’ve never heard of your teachers before, but it’s nice to hear you all reminisce about the midcentury of our last century. I see a familiar pattern here, where many of you feel that famous and successful actors who have attended HB should be contributing to keep HB alive and in place. Some wonder why they didn’t gather to raise money and “SAVE HB.” Well, I ask first and foremost: have any of you here made a recent donation to SAVE HB? I'm aware you probably don’t have the millions of dollars that many of those previously famous students could easily write a check to HB for. But you could certainly write a check to cover the little things that, as you all know, add up to a lot. They may need paint, a computer, reams of paper, a front doorbell, books, and other supplies that your donation could help them secure. A piano. Lightbulbs. Even donate to the petty cash box, provided you trust the current management and Board of directors, which this article seems to have avoided as a possible cautionary tale common in small non-profit or for-profit community institutions.
Gather and create your own “SAVE HB” campaign. Something! As we all know, in community, everyone has a place. Besides complaining here, what is your place in HB history? It has to be more than a memory of when entertainment was black and white!

articles.title: Uta Hagen and Herbert Berghof Played Here. Now the Curtain May Come Down.
articles.byline: John Freeman Gill and Graham Dickie
articles.summary: HB Studio, founded in 1945, has serious financial woes and is in disrepair.

articles.title: Goliath Roller-Coaster Death Casts Long Shadow Over Six Flags’ Turnaround Hopes
articles.byline: Jacob Passy, Allison Pohle and Chip Cutter
articles.summary: It is a make-or-break moment for the amusement-park operator, which has struggled since a July 2024 merger.

comments.name: David Soley
comments.body: I hope using souind judgment that Six Flags leadership to keep costs di not use LLM to write the software for these rides.  Six Flags leadership needs to reassure and acknowledge all their customers that they do not use AI to write software for each ride......and rather quickly.

comments.name: steve coon
comments.body: The first question I have is whether any of the riders were at fault--acting in ways that increased their risk of injury or death?  The company's may be to blame.  But I tend to suspect human misbehavior first.  Condolences to the family.

comments.name: Vince carapellotti
comments.body: This particular park is way past its due date.  Not sure about how good their maintenance is on the rides but the park itself is surrounded by crime - and has been for many years.

comments.name: Dan Micklos
comments.body: Perhaps we all should wait until the investigation is concluded before passing judgement. I am a large man. But I have never had any issues riding amusement park rides such as this one. A disclaimer is in order here; At 69 years old, my wife and I carefully read the warning signs that are usually at the entrance to the attraction. We now pass on many rides. Also, did the deceased person have any role ins being ejected? Let the investigation play out. I can't imagine that there are numerous videos of this ride. It's time to wait and see before assigning blame.

comments.name: Jim McDonough
comments.body:
Dangerous roller coasters?  That's nothing.  Did you go to Action Park in Vernon NJ back in the 1980s as a teen.  I would say "hold my beer" but the kids running the beer garden back then did not care if you were of age, below age, or anything in between.

The deadly wave pool.  The Tarzan rope swings into the frigid, spring-fed water.  People jumping from the platforms 15 feet into the water & landing on someone who did not move fast enough.  The speedboat area infested with water snakes.  At least we HOPED they were water snakes & not something more deadly.

Memories.  Like the corners of my mind.

comments.name: Howard Howes
comments.body: 6 Flags needs to replace the bean counters and install the ANSI BOCA Code ISO Safety Bean Counters. Yes, safety fixes will cost money, but then you will not be in the News for people falling out of Rides.

comments.name: Jerome Feldman
comments.body:
"....and all feature the same clamshell-style lap-bar safety restraints."

But you have to wear a seatbelt and shoulder harness to go 45 mph in a car...

(Mrs. JF)

comments.name: Ellen Shapley
comments.body: Years ago as a skinny 13 year old  riding the Wild Mouse in Seattle, I experienced the terrifying feeling that I was going to be flung out of the car as it went around the curves.  Everyone said, well that ‘s the ride.  But I had ridden the Wild Mouse before in different locations and never experienced anything like that.  I can still feel the panic.

comments.name: Aktrsandr
comments.body: The US intelligence community loathes Russia and will continue to share intelligence with Ukraine, just as it has been doing. Ukraine will continue to use Starlink, just as it has been doing. Musk almost certainly did not make the decision to disable Starlink on his own.

comments.name: populistcurious
comments.body:
Fuel prices don't concern me much, a small price at the pump. Removing internet support for Ukraine does concern me. Russia is a very dangerous country led by a megalomaniac who has no concern for the millions of lives lost due to his war of choice to capture territory. 

If anything we should be increasing our intelligence cooperation and shipping war materials to Ukraine.

comments.name: Mark hope
comments.body: This is what happens when you depend on a company and an individual like musk who has many pies in the oven and many people he needs to keep happy in order keep growing his wealth. This is why no matter where a corporations headquarters are they truly have no allegiance to anyone but their own business interests

comments.name: RickP
comments.body:
This story should be todays major headline in a large font. 

Looks like Trump just threw Ukraine to the Putin wolves. 

No warning. No explanation. 

One guess: to lower diesel prices (or the expectations thereof) to try to salvage the midterms. 

There is no bottom to how far he'll sink.

comments.name: Roberta
comments.body: If Starshield is a US technology then changing out the  Administration at the midterms is essential for its friendly use. The Internet came out of DoD and was shared.

comments.name: Clayton
comments.body: America and Zelensky wouldn't be having this problem if our commanders in chief were subject to the UCMJ, as they should be in time of war. Article 99 would be a good place to start with Trump as he's a proven master in all manner of conducts unbecoming.

comments.name: APFO
comments.body: The new Democratic House and Senate need to drag Musk to account and consider defunding his businesses.

comments.name: Jake
comments.body: SpaceX is asserting political power over an international conflict and in violation of federal law. The midterms are likely to return control of at least the US House of Representatives to the Democrats. As a result, SpaceX should expect extensive inquiries by the legislative branches of the US government into its actions and decisions. The resulting inquiries can be expected to have negative consequences on the stock price of SpaceX and it’s potential to enter Newmarket in areas that support Ukraine in its defense against the invasion by Russia. My unsolicited advice to Elon Musk: preserve all records and standby for further instructions.

articles.title: What Is Starshield, SpaceX’s Military-Grade Satellite Internet Service?

comments.name: SusanT
comments.body: I lived in Lyon in the early 2000s for about two years and had visited frequently when living in Geneva in the 1990s. One thing we all knew was to not waste our money on La Mere Brezier. In fact a friend recently dined there as was not impressed with one dish on their tasting menu inedible. Perhaps if you are Daniel Boulud the kitchen stands at attention! As many have remarked, there are other restaurants where you can eat exceptional meals and a trip to Les Halles has a couple of them. But to not mention Theodore or Comptoir Abel is inexcusable.

comments.name: MicheleP
comments.body: We visited Lyons, after having visited Paris, and actually now prefer Lyons. It is somewhat smaller, of course, but every bit as beautiful and fascinating as Paris. We especially liked the Basilica, and Vieux Lyons the best. For a return stay, we would choose Lyons: all the genuine experience, but half the hustle and haste of Paris. So much more remains to be experienced there!

comments.name: Out West
comments.body: We visited Lyon many years ago (2010). Fantastic city! Loved exploring the traboules. Our visit was in Oct. Will always remember the absolutely stunning and lengthy open air market along the river.

comments.name: Antoine
comments.body: A very classy exploration of the gourmet town by a gourmet chef. I never saw the Parc de la tête d'or that beautiful. The bord du Rhône are also a must do in Lyon.

comments.name: susie
comments.body:
Over the past 30 yeavrsa, I have been to Lyon 7 times.  3  comments to add:

1.  You can get the TGV directly from CDG to Lyon wihtout having to go through Paris
2.  Some great museums - Beaux Arts, Tissus, Gallo-Roman
3.  I have always avoided Rue des Marroniers but, when I was there this summer, could not get to my reserved restaurant due to post soccer match celebrating and resulting tear gas. Finally figured Marroniers was the safest bc they couldn't tear gas that.  Too my surprise, I had an amzaing meal there!  So you never know.  Did have to run home though to avoid tear gas......

comments.name: Sushidogg
comments.body: Yes a wonderful walking city, and the Botanical Garden is relaxing and serene.   I am surprised not to see reference to the stunning murals throughout the city. They are in a league of their own, especially Fresque des Lyonnais- the massive trompe-l'œil mural depicting 30 influential figures from Lyon's history.	Also Mur des Canut, the largest mural in Europe, showcasing the life of Lyon's silk workers.   Give yourself plenty of time to drink these in; they are a wonderful trip into French culture, savoreuse!

comments.name: Martha
comments.body: I was fortunate to live in Lyon in my late 20s, and keep returning to this marvelous, accessible city. Check out Bill Buford’s memoir, Dirt, for an in-depth view of Lyonnaise restaurant culture and the history of French cooking

comments.name: erwan
comments.body: Good to see Daniel Boulud has been practicing "cuisine minceur". (Lyon might be the "stomach" or "belly" of France but he does not feel like showing it). He is an excellent artisan in the French tradition who has managed to flourish in the US and kept up with the times. Another great accomplishment.  Finally, he may no longer farm but he has planted many seeds.

articles.title: Daniel Boulud’s 5 Favorite Places in Lyon, France
articles.summary: The world-famous chef, who just opened his latest outpost in Manhattan, shares some places he loves in the French city he says “will always be home.”

articles.title: Pope Leo Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery

comments.name: Stephen Zorn
comments.body:
I was a member of the team that renegotiated the Panguna mining agreement on behalf of the newly self-governing Papua New Guinea government in 1974, working with then-Chief Minister Michael Somare and the Bougainvilleans John Momis (then chair of the Constitutional Planning Committee and later Governor and President of Bougainville) and Paul Lapun, then PNG Minister for Mines. To our credit, we ended a tax regime, dictated in 1967 to then-colony PNG by the colonial power Australia, that basically gave away the natural resources for the first 20 years of the mine's life, and introduced a novel and effective "resource-rernt" taxation regime that captured most of the excess profits for the national government. 
   What we failed to do, however, despite the input of Momis and Lapun, was to adequately take into account the needs of the people who lived near the mine—at the time, it was the world's second-largest open-pit mining operation. And we failed to anticipate the cumulative effect, over the two decades between our renegotiation of the agreement and the outbreak of rebellion on Bougainville in the 1990s, of the huge changes to the local environment that would be wrought by the mining operations. Victoria Kim's reporting, and the accompanying photographs, brings that effect into focus. I fear, however, that the new Bougainville government, moving ahead quickly with an obscure corporate partner, will simply repeat our earlier mistakes. Mi sori tumas.

I keep coming back to a dinner conversation I read about amongst some IT moguls where Elon Musk was also present.  Somebody asked Elon why he wanted to colonize Mars. He replied that humanity needed a plan B because we would inevitably destroy ourselves. The majority of the attendees felt that it was a noble cause and then the majority predicted that if that were to happen, AI would be the cause of humanity’s demise.  Then someone followed up and asked Musk “wouldn’t humanity be taking AI along with it to Mars?” At which Musk hesitated, turned pale and replied in the affirmative.

I am cynical about ever-positive announcements of drugs that can extend life, or even cure the cancer, without any description of their side effects. Here is my observation: patients begin chemo with the hope of a cure. After enduring debilitating side effects, they continue treatment because they previously committed to chemotherapy. In contrast, good businessmen are clearheaded about the wisdom of cutting one’s losses. Yes, I sound cold. But I am currently watching a friend who might have lived out her days enjoying her normal pleasures, instead of agreeing to the debilitation wrought by infusion after infusion of chemotherapy.
     Just because the medical establishment offers a “possible cure” or extension of one’s life, albeit marred by nausea, tiredness, depression, etc., does not mean a person must buy it.

My father had lung cancer caught on an x-ray for another minor condition. It was removed surgically with clean margins. Without further treatment,  he has done extremely well for 15 yearsand is still independent in his early 90s. What's interesting is he didn't smoke or drink in an era when many people did. I think back and believe his only exposure was he worked in the aerospace industry and might have been exposed to various solvents and chemicals.

Lung cancer treatment and diagnosis has definitely evolved over time. If you are over 50, have or currently smoked, and did not quit over 15 years ago, ask your doctor about getting a lung CT scan. This is now standard of care. If you quit over 15 years ago and don't have respiratory symptoms, your chances of lung cancer is less.

I'd also add that the rate of lung cancer in younger  Asian American women who have not smoked is rising at a clip. It's not clear why. So if you are younger but having symptoms please ask your doctor about lung cancer.

comments.body:
Thanks for shining light on this fascinating piece of public art!
One note on the name: the translation of “ant-trout-kite” building is a little reductive, as "Arimasuton" is a multi-layered Japanese pun. Its full name is "arimasuton-biru" (蟻鱒鳶ル), and while the characters used to write "arimasutonbi" do indeed mean "ant-trout-kite", "arimasu" is far more recognizable to Japanese speakers as a common verb meaning "there is" or "it exists". In interviews (see Japanese BuzzFeed News), the artist explains the name thus (translated):
“The unusual name was given to me by an artist friend.
The positive-sounding "arimasu" (there is) is followed by the auspicious-sounding "ton," like in "Sheraton" and "Hilton." Wanting to include animal kanji, I chose "ant," "trout," and "kite," which symbolize the earth, water, and sky.”

The negative comment quoted are of a knee jerk variety, and frankly reflected my own initial first impressions. I was put off when I saw pictures of architect Frank Gehry's  Seattle Library, which by comparison would be considered conventional, despite many dissonant features. This is far more irregular in some ways, but I see a distinct Asian quality to the structure. To paraphrase, one might say that the structure is greater than the sum of its parts. The actual purpose or function requires a bit of imagination, the living space reminds me of the captain's quarters of an ancient wooden sailing ship, an example once moored in a Seattle harbor. Today is a time when we would even welcome the mundane, given the state of disarray that is reported daily in the news. This structure has the potential to distract us from a world we may feel we know too much about already. In music, the works of Eric Satie may have a similar provocative resonance, defying convention but with just enough structure to deserve consideration as being legitimate, but with a huge amount of artistic license.

“The scientists draw their inspiration from Unix, a pioneering computer programming language created in the 1970s. Because it was open and simple, Unix attracted a global community of computer scientists who used it to innovate.”

This seems unlikely. The UNIX operating system was created in Bell Labs in the early 1970s. The OS was, itself, written in a then new programming language call “C.” UNIX was a purely commercial product, requiring licensing, for a couple of decades. In the early 1990s a Finnish computer science student, Linus Torvalds, wanting the functionality of UNIX without the fees, wrote his own OS, Linux. Linux was released as Open Source, a fairly new concept at the time. Anyone could download the source code via the nascent Internet and compile it themselves. This was the one-thousand-flowers-bloom moment and tens of thousands of people - from computer scientists to hobbyists – began the innovation the article refers to. There is a great deal more to the story. The open source movement, for instance, predates Torvald’s work. It began with the GNU project and a young man named Richard Stallman in the early 1980s. But that is a story for another day . . .

I understand the negative comments. But for me, it's about meeting people. Not just actors or writers or artists. The fans. Waiting in line, striking up conversations with the people around me, sharing experiences, and cordially debating the merits of whatever or whomever we are in line to see. No matter our differences, we share a passion for the films, shows, books and art that are the blood of the con.

This year I met Nicholas Cage (albeit briefly), Christian Slater, Peter Weller, Nancy Allen, Terry Brooks (again, because he's awesome), Rosario Dawson, Hayden Christensen, and more. Yes, I pay for those autographs, but I came away with experiences I can share countless times. I also collected some books, met some authors I have never read before but will now, and a couple of pieces of artwork. And in every one of those lines, I got to chat with fans of all kinds, shared laughter and commiserated about the wait that we all forgot about when we reached the front.

Is it expensive? Yup, sure is. Is it exhausting and occasionally frustrating? Heck yes. But it is also an exhilarating, joyful celebration of fandom, 30,000 people letting their nerd flag fly high and proud. I'll be there again next year, the guy happy to be in line with you.

comments.name: SheCando
comments.body:
The obscene concentration of wealth at the top of this company is unfathomable. And it’s not just Ted and Greg, it’s the entire C-suite and VP level, where compensation has become completely detached from reality.

I know people in comparable roles who would earn $300–500K elsewhere (still very healthy salaries in LA) but are making $2–3 million at Netflix. Meanwhile, managers and below have gone years without raises and survived  (or not!) year after year of layoffs, and now this, pushing hundreds more people into an already oversaturated and brutal job market.

At what point does corporate citizenship come into this? Why are the people at the top seemingly insulated from the consequences of their own decisions, while everyone else is expected to absorb the cost? If employees are held accountable for performance and the company’s financial priorities, shouldn’t that apply just as much to the executives making the decisions?

The solution isn’t complicated: tie executive compensation to the company’s actual performance and long-term health AND cap excessive pay at the top. A company this successful should be able to do better by its people. It’s hard to justify a system where the rewards keep flowing upward while the consequences are pushed downward.

I loved watching him, it was a puzzle, except with live wires. That kind of improvising in messy, real buildings is what I think AI can't replace soon. I'm exactly who the article worries about: I love CS and math, and I've read that Indian IT firms like TCS have cut fresher hiring as automation handles entry level code. So yes, I'd learn a trade, probably electrical work, but as a second skill, not my whole career. If I told my parents "electrician" was the plan, they'd think I was joking. comments.name: August Cortez
comments.body: I agree that learning a trade can be a good way to plan a career, especially as AI continues to change the jobs in the market. While AI is becoming a fast way of completing many tasks, careers like electricians, plumbers, and construction workers require human experience and problem-solving skills that technology cannot easily replace. In the article, LaDonna Glass explains how she left college to pursue an apprenticeship as an electrician. Instead of spending thousands on tuition, she's earning money while learning valuable skills. Her experience shows that success does not always require a college degree. I also believe that society puts too much pressure on students to attend college immediately after high school. Although college gives students good opportunities, it shouldn't be seen as the only path to a successful future. Trade schools allow students to get good experience, develop useful skills, and maybe avoid large amounts of student debt. However, I don't think learning a trade makes sure you're protected from AI because technology is constantly evolving. Personally, I would still consider attending college, but I do respect those who choose to go to a trade school. Ultimately, I believe students should pursue careers that match their interests and strengths rather than feeling pressured to follow a traditional path.

This means that while nearly 4 in 10 Americans have a college degree, only about a quarter of those graduates are employed in directly related positions. But, roughly 86% of people who enroll in trade school are employed in their field within a year of completion. So, for many people trade school is a much better option for their money and time.

Her memory care facility held a talent show, and my sister and mom dressed up in full costume and did ballet together - it was incredibly beautiful to see my mom so engaged with the pastime she never stopped loving.

I really love it and wish I had found recreational ballet 20 years ago when I was raising babies and needed an outlet. Most of my fellow students are in their 30s and I am so happy that they won't have the same decades-long break-up from ballet that I had.

Hopper was a very visual artist - a realist who painted what he saw, and focused on the light and colors and shapes in front of him. His seacoast paintings in bright sunlight are nothing like his late-night city scenes because the light and the settings are different. If a Hopper  painting tells a story it is because the viewer is looking at it through their own imagination. That doesn’t diminish his work, which I love.

comments.name: tyrdofwaitin

I've been an ardent fan of Hopper's work since childhood.  In part because his locales are so familiar---I grew up in Greenwich Village and vacationed in New England---but because at a very young age, I immediately recongnized Hooper's world: pristine isolation.  I see paper mache like white figures who silently weep loss and loneliness.  As an adult, I came to realize that Hopper had captured the emptiness of American individualism better than anybody I know.

Yes it's Puritan, and Anglo-Saxon, and fundamentalist, patriarchal, hegemonic---our founding ethos although we continue to deny it.  It's no surprise that his personal life mirrored this.  Hopper, the truth teller.

The reaction of Israel to the barbarism of a small group of terrorists did not justify the destruction of Gaza with far more people killed and the overwhelming destruction of the territory. Who but the International Criminal Court can bring a semblance of justice for the victims? Only through evidence can the crimes of Hamas and Israel’s overwrought response to that attack provide pathways for all parties to be held accountable. Perhaps, through the catharsis of evidence and memory, all parties can forge a better path forward. The world has been galvanized by these events. We all have been exposed to the violence. It is time to accept the next stage of our evolution as people existing on a planet and not merely nations and city-states. The 
ICC is a good place to bring accountability to violence and murder by states and countries. Only through exposure of the true facts of events such as the destruction of Gaza, of countries attacking one another, of violence to people by rebel armies can we build consensus against violence as a means to an end. All voices and stories need to be heard and told. The actions by trump to penalize the ICC does not represent our democracy or the foundations of our government. Not mentioned here is that Park Chung-hee is also despised by many on the South Korean political left for his perceived willingness to collaborate with the Japanese colonial authorities when he was a young soldier in the 1940s. It's now clear to me that the Korean War (1950-53) was not so much a conflict between advocates of communism and capitalism as it was a conflict between those (the people calling themselves communists in the North) who saw themselves as having fully resisted Japanese colonial rule against those in the South who were perceived as traitorous, opportunistic pro-Japanese collaborators and turncoats backed by a U.S. government willing to turn a blind eye.
